questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painless ulcer on the glans penis with indurated, clean base and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark field microscopy shows spirochetes. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents with a painless, indurated (hard) chancre with a clean base. Dark field microscopy demonstrating motile spirochetes is the gold standard for diagnosis of Treponema pallidum, the causative agent.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with multiple painless ulcers in the inguinal region. Gram stain shows intracellular 'Donovan bodies' within mononuclear cells. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks
questions.exp: Donovan bodies (intracellular Klebsiella granulomatis within macrophages) are diagnostic of Donovanosis (Granuloma inguinale). First-line treatment is Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks until all lesions have healed. Azithromycin is an alternative.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy (MDT) develops sudden onset painful, hot, red nodules on the face and extremities with fever and joint pains. Skin biopsy shows diffuse neutrophilic infiltrate. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Type 2 lepra reaction (ENL) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated reaction presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate. Treatment is thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with bilateral symmetric hypopigmented anesthetic patches on the trunk. Slit skin smear shows a bacteriological index (BI) of 2+. According to WHO classification, this patient has:
questions.exp: WHO classifies leprosy as multibacillary (MB) if BI ≥1+ on slit skin smear at any site. MB leprosy requires 12-month MDT with rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone. PB leprosy has BI of 0 and ≤5 patches.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are also positive. Renal biopsy shows mesangial deposits. She is most likely to respond to:
questions.exp: This patient has SLE with mesangial nephritis (Class II lupus nephritis), which is relatively mild. Hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone of SLE management, combined with low-dose prednisolone for active disease. Aggressive immunosuppression (MMF/cyclophosphamide) is reserved for Class III/IV nephritis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing Raynaud's phenomenon develops sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, and dysphagia. Her anti-centromere antibodies are positive. She is most likely to develop which complication?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome). This subtype has a high risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and interstitial lung disease.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the inner thighs and flexures. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae (subepidermal) on normal or erythematous skin, preferring flexures. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ (lamina lucida). Autoantibodies target BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230. Pemphigus shows intraepidermal split with IgG in intercellular pattern.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with flaccid bullae and erosions on the oral mucosa for 3 months followed by skin involvement. Nikolsky's sign is positive. The target antigen of the autoantibodies is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) predominantly involves mucous membranes first, then skin, with flaccid bullae. Autoantibodies target Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type). Desmoglein 1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus (superficial, skin-only). Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A patient on long-term phenytoin therapy for epilepsy develops a diffuse, erythematous, maculopapular rash with fever and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory shows eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes. The most likely diagnosis is:
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) presents 2-8 weeks after drug initiation. It features morbilliform rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, and internal organ involvement (liver most common). Aromatic anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) are classic causative drugs.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with well-demarcated scaly plaques on the scalp, elbows, and knees. The Koebner phenomenon is positive. Auspitz sign is positive. The pathological finding underlying the Auspitz sign is:
opts: Dilated capillary loops in elongated dermal papillae
questions.exp: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removal of psoriatic scale) results from dilated and tortuous capillary loops in elongated dermal papillae that are exposed when scales are removed. Munro's microabscesses are neutrophilic collections in the stratum corneum, characteristic of psoriasis histologically.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with ring-shaped pruritic lesions with central clearing on her trunk. KOH examination shows branching hyphae with arthroconidia. The most appropriate treatment is:
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (ringworm of the body) shows annular lesions with active scaly border and central clearing. KOH shows hyphae. Terbinafine (allylamine) is first-line for dermatophytosis - it is fungicidal with shorter treatment duration. Fluconazole dosing for tinea is typically 150 mg weekly, but terbinafine has superior efficacy.

questions.q: A 22-year-old immunocompetent man presents with hypopigmented macules on the chest and upper back with fine scaling. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH preparation shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor (Pityriasis versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (a lipophilic yeast). KOH shows short hyphae and spores resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green or copper-orange fluorescence. Treatment includes selenium sulfide, topical azoles, or oral itraconazole.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child develops grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution preceded by prodromal pain. The rash resolves but the child continues to have severe burning pain in that area. The pathophysiology involves:
opts: Reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia
Primary HSV-1 infection of sensory neurons
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) is caused by reactivation of Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) that remained latent in dorsal root ganglia (or cranial nerve ganglia) after primary varicella infection. In children, shingles may follow perinatal varicella. Post-herpetic neuralgia is the persistent pain after rash resolution.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with multiple soft, skin-colored papules with central umbilication on the genitalia and inner thighs. The lesions are positive for molluscum bodies on Giemsa stain. The causative virus belongs to:
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxvirus family. The Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies are pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusions seen on histology. In sexually active adults, anogenital location suggests STD transmission.

questions.q: A newborn presents with vesiculopustular lesions in a linear distribution along Blaschko's lines associated with eosinophilia. The mother had similar vesicles during pregnancy that resolved. Biopsy shows intraepidermal eosinophilic spongiosis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) follows Blaschko's lines and has 4 stages: (1) vesicular/inflammatory, (2) verrucous, (3) hyperpigmented, (4) hypopigmented atrophic. Stage 1 shows eosinophilic vesicles and peripheral eosinophilia. IP is X-linked dominant (IKBKG/NEMO gene) and usually lethal in males.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the nose. She has a history of chronic sun exposure. The most likely diagnosis and its recommended treatment are:
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma; wide local excision
Basal cell carcinoma; Mohs micrographic surgery
questions.exp: Nodular BCC presents as a pearly, translucent papule/nodule with rolled borders, surface telangiectasia, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer) on sun-exposed skin. On the nose (H-zone face), Mohs micrographic surgery is the gold standard for complete margin assessment and maximal tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with an ulcerated, keratotic nodule on the dorsum of the hand with regional lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which feature indicates the worst prognosis?
questions.exp: Perineural invasion (PNI) in SCC is a high-risk feature associated with increased recurrence, regional metastasis, and mortality. Other high-risk features include: depth >2mm, Clark level ≥IV, poor differentiation, location on ear/lip, size >2cm, arising in chronic wounds or immunosuppression.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a changing, asymmetric pigmented lesion on her back with irregular borders. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Observe for 3 months and repeat dermoscopy
Punch biopsy from the darkest area
questions.exp: Suspected melanoma requires excisional biopsy with 1-2 mm margins to assess Breslow thickness (the most important prognostic factor) and other histologic features. Shave biopsy is contraindicated as it transects the lesion and prevents accurate Breslow depth measurement.

questions.q: A patient presents with multiple cafe-au-lait macules (>6, each >1.5 cm), axillary freckling, and multiple soft subcutaneous nodules along peripheral nerves. The gene mutation underlying this condition is in:
questions.exp: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1/von Recklinghausen disease) is caused by mutations in NF1 gene (chromosome 17q11.2) encoding neurofibromin (a tumor suppressor/RAS-GTPase). Diagnostic features include ≥6 CALMs >1.5 cm, axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign), neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, and gliomas.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman develops a bullous eruption with healing of lesions leaving milia and scarring, predominantly on the dorsum of hands and other trauma-prone areas. She has no mucosal involvement. Type VII collagen antibodies are detected. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is an autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease with autoantibodies against Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils at the BMZ). Classic form is non-inflammatory, mechanobullous on trauma-prone sites with milia and scarring. DIF shows IgG at the BMZ on salt-split skin at the dermal side.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with extremely pruritic vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Small bowel biopsy shows subtotal villous atrophy. Serology reveals anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. The drug that is most rapidly effective for skin symptoms is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips. Dapsone provides rapid (within days) relief of pruritus and suppresses lesions, while a strict gluten-free diet is the definitive long-term treatment.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man develops erythematous patches with silvery-white scales that fluoresce under Wood's lamp. Tzanck smear shows no giant cells. The condition responds to narrow-band UVB. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Psoriasis presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white (micaceous) scales, positive Auspitz sign, and Koebner phenomenon. It does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp (that feature belongs to other conditions). Narrow-band UVB (311 nm) is an effective phototherapy for psoriasis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old diabetic woman presents with hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of the skin in the axillae and neck folds. This is associated with hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance. The correct term for this condition is:
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans presents as hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in body folds (axillae, neck, groin). It is associated with insulin resistance (T2DM, obesity, PCOS) and rarely malignancy (sign of Leser-Trélat when rapid onset). The mechanism involves insulin binding to IGF-1 receptors stimulating keratinocyte proliferation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with bilateral, symmetric hyperpigmented patches on the cheeks and forehead that worsen with sun exposure and pregnancy. Wood's lamp examination shows enhancement of pigmentation. The treatment with the strongest evidence is:
questions.exp: Melasma is a common acquired hypermelanosis, worsened by UV, pregnancy, and OCPs. Kligman's formula (triple combination cream: HQ 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the gold standard topical treatment with extensive evidence for efficacy. Strict photoprotection is essential.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with erythema, papules, and scales around the hair follicles on the scalp, elbows, and knees. The scales contain a brittle inner hair that breaks at the follicular opening creating a 'corkscrew' appearance. This finding is pathognomonic of:
questions.exp: Perifollicular hemorrhages and corkscrew (swan-neck) hairs are pathognomonic of Scurvy (Vitamin C/ascorbic acid deficiency). Vitamin C is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis. Other features include bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and Woody leg. Phrynoderma (follicular hyperkeratosis) is caused by Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with extensive psoriasis is started on methotrexate. After 2 years of treatment, the cumulative dose reaches 3.5g. The mandatory investigation to assess treatment-related organ toxicity at this stage is:
questions.exp: Methotrexate causes hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis with long-term use. Traditional guidelines recommend liver biopsy at a cumulative dose of 1.5g (or earlier if risk factors) and every 1-1.5g thereafter. However, non-invasive tests like Fibrometer, FIB-4, or transient elastography are increasingly used as alternatives, but liver biopsy remains the gold standard reference.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male patient presents with grouped pruritic papules and vesicles on the interdigital web spaces, wrists, and periumbilical area. His partner has similar lesions. KOH of the burrow scrapings shows the mite. The treatment of choice for the patient and all close contacts is:
opts: 5% permethrin cream applied from neck to toes, washed after 8-14 hours
Benzyl benzoate 25% applied for 3 consecutive nights
Topical crotamiton 10% cream applied twice daily for 5 days
questions.exp: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei. First-line treatment is 5% permethrin cream (applied from neck downward, left for 8-14 hours, repeated after 1 week). It is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months. Oral ivermectin is an effective alternative for crusted scabies or mass treatment. All contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer with violaceous undermined edges on the lower limb that has been slowly expanding over 3 months. Biopsy shows suppurative granulomas with 'double contoured' thick-walled yeast cells. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: North American blastomycosis presents with chronic verrucous or ulcerated lesions with violaceous undermined borders. Histopathology shows broad-based budding yeast with thick, double-contoured cell wall (unlike the narrow-based budding in Cryptococcus and Histoplasma). Treatment is itraconazole for mild-moderate disease and amphotericin B for severe disease.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a linear ascending nodular lymphangitis on the forearm following a thorn prick while gardening. Biopsy of a nodule grows a dimorphic fungus at 25°C showing asteroid bodies. The treatment of choice is:
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) classically presents as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis with nodular lymphangitis following inoculation trauma. Asteroid bodies are seen in tissue. Itraconazole 200 mg/day for 3-6 months is the current treatment of choice. SSKI was historically used but itraconazole is now preferred for its tolerability.

questions.q: During a patch test for contact allergy in a patient with eczema, the optimal time to apply and read the patch test results is:
opts: Apply for 24 hours, read at 24 and 48 hours
Apply for 48 hours, read at 48 and 96 hours
Apply for 72 hours, read at 72 and 96 hours
Apply for 48 hours, read at 48, 72, and 96 hours
questions.exp: Standard patch test protocol (European/ICDRG): patches are applied to the upper back and left in place for 48 hours, then removed. First reading at 48 hours (removal), second reading at 96 hours (D4), sometimes a third at D7 for late reactions (especially to metals and neomycin). The 96-hour reading is most important for clinical relevance.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with a history of recurrent oral herpes labialis develops sudden onset severe blistering of the lips, oral mucosa, conjunctiva, and skin with widespread targetoid lesions and mucosal erosions. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Supportive care + acyclovir 400 mg twice daily long-term prophylaxis
questions.exp: This describes HSV-triggered Stevens-Johnson syndrome (or recurrent Erythema Multiforme Major). HSV is the commonest trigger of EM and SJS. The key in HSV-associated EM/SJS is prevention with long-term acyclovir prophylaxis (400mg BD for 6-12 months or longer), which dramatically reduces recurrences. Systemic steroids are controversial in SJS.
